title: Why Do 1 in 3 People Get Carsick? 🚗
description:
Why do some people get carsick while others can read in the back seat? Motion sickness explained in simple words: how your eyes and inner ear (the vestibular system) disagree, the poison theory, the genes behind it, and why the driver almost never feels sick.

Sources:
https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/motion-sickness/
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383869/

topic: Why do some people get carsick and others don't?
script: Every time you get carsick, your brain thinks you've swallowed poison. And for one in three people, that alarm goes off on almost every ride. So why does the back seat wreck some of us, while others read a whole book and feel totally fine? To find out, we need to look inside your head. You know how you're moving using two main systems. Your eyes are one. The other is hidden deep inside each ear. It's called the vestibular system, and it's basically a built-in motion sensor. Three tiny loops filled with fluid sense every time your head turns. And two little sacs lined with tiny crystals feel you speed up, slow down and tip. Most of the time your eyes and ears agree. But picture yourself in the back seat, reading a phone. Your eyes see a screen that isn't moving. Your inner ear feels every bump and every curve. One says still. The other says moving. Scientists call this sensory conflict, and it's the leading explanation for motion sickness. So why would a mixed-up signal make you feel sick? One popular theory goes way back to our ancestors. Long ago, if your senses suddenly stopped agreeing, a likely cause was something toxic you'd eaten. So the brain may have learned a simple rule. Signals don't match? Empty the stomach. Researchers still debate this idea, but it would explain why a bumpy ride can feel a lot like food poisoning. Here's where it gets personal. In 2015 the genetics company 23andMe studied more than eighty thousand people. They found thirty-five spots in our DNA linked to motion sickness. And some studies suggest up to seventy percent of the difference between people comes down to genes. Age matters too. Kids between about seven and twelve get it the most, and lots of people grow out of the worst of it. Women report it more often than men, and so do people who get migraines. So if your whole family turns green on road trips, that's probably not a coincidence. Now for the strangest part. People who have completely lost the motion sensors in their inner ears basically don't get motion sick at all. No inner ear signal, no conflict, no alarm. What you can see matters too. One study found that passengers who couldn't see the road ahead were about three times more likely to feel sick. And the driver? Usually fine. The driver knows every turn before it happens, so the brain isn't caught by surprise. This old alarm is now facing brand new problems. Virtual reality flips the conflict around. Your eyes see motion, but your body sits perfectly still. And as cars start driving themselves, everyone becomes a passenger, staring at screens instead of the road. So engineers are testing tricks, like lights that hint at the next turn, to help your eyes and ears agree again. So the next time a car ride makes you queasy, remember, your brain isn't broken. It's just protecting you from a poison that isn't there. Next time, what really happens if a porcupine's quills get stuck in you?
key_facts: About 1 in 3 people are highly susceptible to motion sickness (MedlinePlus; Hromatka et al. 2015)
The leading explanation is sensory conflict: eyes signal still while the inner ear signals moving
One theory: the brain treats the mismatch like a sign of poisoning and triggers nausea (debated)
A 2015 23andMe study of 80,494 people found 35 genetic variants linked to motion sickness
Heritability estimates for motion sickness range up to about 70%
Children about 7-12 are most susceptible; it is more common in women and in people with migraines
People with complete loss of vestibular function are essentially immune to motion sickness
Passengers without a view of the road ahead were about 3 times more likely to get sick
